title: Health & pharmacy
body:
Emergency numbers: Police 110, Fire/Ambulance 119 — both work nationwide, English support is limited but dispatchers can usually connect a translator. Save these before you land; this guide's travel-advisory field couldn't be independently confirmed this research pass (see the note below), so treat this as the baseline safety info rather than a substitute for a live check closer to travel.

Pharmacies (drugstores — Matsumoto Kiyoshi, Sugi, Tsuruha) are everywhere in Tenjin, Susukino, and around Sendai Station, but English-speaking pharmacists are the exception outside Tokyo — bring any prescriptions in their original labeled packaging, and a doctor's note if you carry anything that could read as a controlled substance (some common US allergy/ADHD medications are restricted in Japan).

Hokkaido and Tohoku in late Oct/Nov run cold — Sapporo's average first snow lands late October, and mountain trail areas (Jozankei's harder routes, Zao) can see snow well before that. Pack real layers and waterproof footwear for the hiking days, not just a light jacket.

Earthquakes: Japan is seismically active nationwide, and Tohoku specifically was the epicenter region of the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake — several of this trip's Tohoku stops (Naruko Gorge's shortened trail, coastal Matsushima) still carry visible aftereffects. If a quake hits while you're there: drop, cover, hold on; away from the coast there's no tsunami risk, but Matsushima's a coastal stop — know the nearest high ground if you're there when one happens.

US State Dept travel advisory: could not be independently confirmed this research pass — its page is bot-gated against automated fetches and needs a live browser check. Widely (but not primary-source-confirmed) reported as Level 1 (Exercise Normal Precautions) as of mid-2025. Check travel.state.gov directly before you go.
